subject: chemistry_2
question_text: How do you prepare the following? i) N,N-dimethylpropanamine from ammonia  ii) Propanamine from chloroethane

verification.note: Unit 18 (Organic Compounds Containing Nitrogen) is sourced from the chemistry half of "FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students", book pp.115-120, from the shaded sub-box "ORGANIC COMPOUNDS CONTAINING NITROGEN" of printed chapter 12 ("12. ORGANIC CHEMISTRY"); the book prints this question on book p.116 as SAQ 3. The 2+2 mark split is a CLAIM, not the board's, until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. Neither the two-book union check nor a board back-test was possible for Chemistry-II: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is physics-only and first-year, and no second-year chemistry paper is in the corpus. BOOK ERROR, corrected on this card: two of the printed equations do not balance. The book writes "NH₃ + C₃H₇Cl → C₃H₇–NH₂" with the chlorine simply gone; with excess ammonia the balanced form is C₃H₇Cl + 2NH₃ → C₃H₇NH₂ + NH₄Cl. It also writes "CH₃–CH₂Cl —NaCN, ethanolic→ CH₃CH₂CN" with the sodium and the chlorine gone; the balanced form is C₂H₅Cl + NaCN → C₂H₅CN + NaCl. Both are written balanced here. BOOK GAPS, filled here: (1) the book does not say that EXCESS ammonia is used in the first step, which is what keeps further alkylation down; (2) it does not say that route (ii) works because the cyanide route ADDS one carbon — chloroethane has two carbons and propanamine has three, so simple ammonolysis of chloroethane could never give it.

steps.label: From ammonia
lines: Ammonia is alkylated three times over: once
Excess ammonia is used in the first step so
that most of the halide meets ammonia and
steps.why: Ammonolysis replaces one hydrogen of ammonia at a time, so each alkyl group needs its own halide and its own step. The order matters: the propyl group is put on first from 1-chloropropane, then the two methyl groups from chloromethane. Ammonia is a nucleophile and the halide supplies the alkyl group.
common_mistakes: Writing the first step with the chlorine simply left out. With excess ammonia it leaves as ammonium chloride, so the equation balances.
Adding all three alkyl groups in one arrow. Each substitution is a separate step with its own halide.
steps.memory_tip: Propyl on first, then methyl, then methyl again. Three groups on nitrogen need three separate arrows.
steps.margin_note: Three balanced equations carry these two marks. Naming the final product in words finishes the answer.

steps.label: From chloroethane
lines: propanamine has three, so one carbon must
be added. The cyanide route does that.
steps.why: The cyanide ion adds its own carbon atom to the chain, so the chain grows from two carbons to three. Reducing the nitrile then converts –C≡N into –CH₂–NH₂ without changing the chain length again. Ammonolysis of chloroethane could not be used, because it would give ethanamine with only two carbons.
common_mistakes: Treating chloroethane with ammonia. That gives ethanamine, which has two carbons, not three.
Leaving the sodium chloride out of the first equation. The equation must balance in sodium and chlorine as well as carbon.
steps.memory_tip: Cyanide adds a carbon, reduction adds four hydrogens. Two carbons in, three carbons out.
steps.margin_note: Count the carbons in the question first: if the product is longer than the starting material, the cyanide route is the one wanted.

insider_note: Part (ii) is a counting question before it is a chemistry question — chloroethane has two carbons and propanamine has three, so a route that adds a carbon is needed and only the cyanide route does that. Both printed equations in the book are unbalanced; write yours with NH₄Cl and NaCl on the right.
